title: Similar Areas and Volumes

findings.finding: Recovering length ratios from area or volume ratios is required without teaching the inverse relationship.
findings.breakdown: The first reverse-area task, p6-q3c-node, requires taking the square root of 45/20 before scaling a length. Later table rows require choosing square roots or cube roots according to the supplied quantity. Applying the area or volume factor directly to lengths is a plausible error.
findings.checked: All supplied teaching was checked. p4-information and its example and guided practice demonstrate only forward area scaling. p9-ratio-definition and its example and guided practice demonstrate only forward volume scaling. Earlier reverse-area practice requires this missing method but does not teach it. Finding an original volume from a known linear factor reverses proportional scaling, not the power relationship.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary square and cube roots are prior arithmetic knowledge. Calculator access does not supply the decision about which inverse operation connects the quantities. Geometric length ratios are positive.

repair.proposal: Before p6-q3c-node add: 'To recover a length ratio from an area ratio, take square roots of both terms. Areas 8 cm² and 18 cm² have ratio 4:9, so corresponding lengths have ratio √4:√9 = 2:3. A length of 6 cm on the smaller figure corresponds to 6 × 3/2 = 9 cm.' Before p12-q12-root add: 'To recover a length ratio from a volume ratio, take cube roots of both terms. Volume ratio 8:27 gives length ratio ∛8:∛27 = 2:3, then area ratio 2²:3² = 4:9.'

findings.doneWhen: Square-root and cube-root recovery are each modelled before their first required use, with the operation explicitly connected to the quantity supplied.

findings.finding: Use a second drawing of the same playground to connect a change in drawing scale with the squared area multiplier.
findings.breakdown: The real playground remains unchanged while its diagram lengths double, making its diagram area four times as large.
findings.checked: The original scale is 1 cm = 10 m and the proposed scale is 2 cm = 10 m. Corresponding diagram lengths therefore double, and 4 × 4.3 = 17.2 cm². This uses the area scaling taught in p4-information and p4-example-triangle.
findings.assumptions: The playground represents the same real region in both drawings.

repair.proposal: After p6-q4c-node, add part d: “The same park is redrawn using a scale of 2 cm = 10 m. What area does the playground occupy on the new diagram? Explain why.” Expected answer: 17.2 cm²; the diagram lengths double, so its area is multiplied by 2² = 4.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up appears as part d of the existing park question with the expected answer 17.2 cm².

findings.finding: Compare the combined surface area of the smaller balls with the surface area of the original ball.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects conservation of volume with the different scaling of surface area.
findings.checked: A radius ratio of 1:5 gives a surface-area ratio of 1:25 and a volume ratio of 1:125. Consequently, 125 smaller balls have combined surface area 125/25 = 5 times the original. Both scaling relationships are available by the end of this topic; no sphere formula is required.
findings.assumptions: The existing task assumes that all the original metal becomes the 125 smaller solid balls without loss.

repair.proposal: After the existing question, add (b): “What fraction of the original ball’s surface area does one smaller ball have?” Expected answer: 1/25. Add (c): “How many times the original ball’s surface area is the combined surface area of all 125 smaller balls?” Expected answer: 5 times.

findings.doneWhen: The two separate follow-up parts retain the original ball context and have expected answers 1/25 and 5 times.

findings.finding: The introductory numerical ratios do not distinguish squaring both terms from squaring only the second term.
findings.breakdown: The wrong rule a:b → a:b² gives the demonstrated introductory results because every first term is 1. It gives 4:25 instead of 16:25 in p7-q7-a.
findings.checked: p3-investigation, p4-example-triangle and p4-guided use ratios beginning with 1. p4-information states the correct symbolic rule, but no worked numerical contrast or guided question exposes the wrong rule before independent practice.
findings.assumptions: Students may infer the operation from the numerical demonstrations; the symbolic statement alone does not expose this special case under the review standard.

repair.proposal: After p4-example-triangle add: 'Square both terms: a length ratio of 2:3 gives an area ratio of 2²:3² = 4:9, not 2:9.'

findings.doneWhen: Introductory teaching explicitly distinguishes squaring both ratio terms from squaring only the second.

findings.finding: Extend the statue question by comparing it with a second similar model.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects doubling corresponding lengths with multiplying area by four and volume by eight.
findings.checked: The original statue-to-model volume ratio 27:1 gives a length ratio of 3:1. A second model twice the first model's height therefore has statue-to-second-model volume ratio 27:8 and second-to-first-model surface-area ratio 4:1. Both relationships are available by the end of this topic.
findings.assumptions: The second model is geometrically similar to the statue and the first model.

repair.proposal: Append to p13-q13-root: 'c. A second similar model of the statue is twice the height of the first model. What is the volume ratio of the statue to the second model?' Answer: 27:8. 'd. What is the surface-area ratio of the second model to the first model?' Answer: 4:1.

findings.doneWhen: The two follow-up parts are appended, explicitly specifying a similar second model.
